name: Cold water / ice to close pores

lead: Many skin-care routines end with a cold splash or a rub of ice, on the belief that cold closes pores that warmth opened, so skin looks tighter and pores look smaller.

Practitioners describe cold as tightening the skin. Dermatology references describe pores as the openings of hair follicles where sebum and keratin can form a plug, and they do not describe pores opening and closing. No published trial testing cold water or ice on pore size was identified.

paras: People finish cleansing with a splash of cold water, or wrap ice in a cloth and glide it over the face for a short time. It is also used to reduce morning puffiness and as a post-steam step.
Brief cold exposure is generally low risk. Prolonged direct ice contact on skin can irritate it, per general dermatology cautions.

chain: Cold splash or ice on face
angle.text: Splashing the face with cold water or rubbing ice on it is a long-circulating routine step meant to close pores and leave skin looking tighter. The idea comes from tradition, and no trials were found testing it.

lead: The belief that splashing the face with cold water or rubbing ice on it makes pores close or shrink is a long-circulating skin-care idea. Proponents describe pores as opening with warmth and closing with cold.

Dermatology references describe pores as the openings of hair follicles, where sebum and keratin can form a plug called a comedo [1][2]. The reference sources reviewed for this article make no statement that pores open or close, and no published trial testing cold water or ice on pore size was identified.

paras: Proponents say that warm water or steam opens pores for cleansing and that a final rinse with cold water or an ice cube closes them and tightens the skin. The practice is often included in skin-care routines as a last step.

Sebaceous glands release sebum onto the hair shaft and skin surface, and sebum and keratin can form a plug in the follicular opening [2]. Blackheads are open comedones, whose dark color is due to oxidation [1]. Dermatology references describe extraction typically being done after steaming or warm washing [1]. Neither source describes pores as having muscles or a mechanism for opening and closing, and neither addresses cold exposure.
